name: Information perception
purpose: Why do decision-makers miss or misread information?

parts.label: Ambiguous cues
points: Meaning is shaped by experience, knowledge, expectations, identity

parts.label: Scarcity vs abundance
points: Too much information → we filter out
Too little → we fill gaps with meaning

example: The moonwalking gorilla video; cell-phone users missing a unicycling clown (Hyman et al. 2010).

parts.label: Bounded rationality
points: Heuristics save mental effort – usually work, not always accurate

parts.label: Key nuance
points: Both run in parallel – both can be correct or biased

name: Categorization biases
purpose: How does putting things into boxes bias judgement?

parts.label: Prototype
points: Categories carry a typical member (“imagine a CEO”, “imagine a book”)

parts.label: In-group favoritism
points: Favour own group, even when randomly assigned

parts.label: Low tolerance of ambiguity (Bochner)
points: Premature closure, rejection of the unusual

apply: A diagnosis is a categorization and a decision is binary – but strategic problems are ambiguous: question each “this is like …”

name: Expertise traps & confirmation bias
purpose: Why can experience make decisions worse?

parts.label: Cognitive entrenchment
points: Experts have rich but stable schemas

parts.label: Einstellung effect
points: Prioritizing the known solution over new, better ones

example: The Bear (TV series): the star chef reaches for fine dining, the solution he knows.

name: Causal thinking: sources of endogeneity
purpose: Can we claim that A causes B?

parts.label: 1. Simultaneity / reverse causation
points: Does B cause A? (police budgets and crime)

parts.label: 2. Omitted (confounding) variable
points: C drives both A and B → spurious correlation (ice cream & sunburn: heat)

parts.label: 3. Measurement error
points: A or B badly measured (money? happiness?)

parts.label: 4. Selection bias
points: Sampling · survivorship · attrition · non-response · volunteer · undercoverage

apply: Ask how the data were generated
Name a plausible reverse cause, a confounder and a selection problem
Propose an experiment (A/B test, natural experiment)
example: Wald's WWII bombers: armour where returning planes were NOT hit. eBay ads mostly reached people who would have bought anyway.

name: Decision quality checklist
purpose: How should a reviewer check a team's recommendation for biases?

parts.label: Questions about the team (self)
points: Affect heuristic (in love with the idea)

parts.label: Questions to the team
points: Anchoring (where do the numbers come from?)

parts.label: Questions about the proposal
points: Over-optimism / planning fallacy / competitor neglect → outside view

pitfalls: Thinking awareness removes bias – it does not
A reviewer who stated a preference early is no longer independent

name: Making groups smarter
purpose: Why do groups amplify errors, and how to fix it?
